title: India Sounds Alarm on Dengue Surge as Monsoon Fuels Record Early-Season Cases
excerpt: With nearly 7,000 dengue cases recorded by February alone and multiple states reporting spikes, the government is rushing to bolster surveillance before the monsoon peak.
body:
• Union Health Minister JP Nadda has directed all states and UTs to strengthen dengue and malaria surveillance ahead of the monsoon season, emphasising early detection and rapid response mechanisms.
  • India recorded 6,927 dengue cases by the end of February 2026 alone — surpassing the full January-May 2021 total within just two months, signalling an alarming year-round transmission trend.
  • Karnataka leads with 5,374 cases and five deaths, followed by Telangana (882 cases) and Ernakulam in Kerala (400 cases), as monsoon rains accelerate mosquito breeding.
  • Health experts warn dengue is no longer a seasonal disease in India, with climate change and urbanisation expanding transmission windows beyond the traditional post-monsoon period.

India is grappling with a surge in dengue and other vector-borne diseases as the monsoon settles in across the subcontinent, prompting the central government to ramp up surveillance systems and direct states to prepare for what health officials warn could be an unusually severe season.

A High-Level Push for Preparedness

Union Health Minister JP Nadda chaired a high-level review meeting in June with senior officials from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to assess preparedness against dengue and malaria. He directed states and Union Territories to intensify surveillance activities, strengthen laboratory testing capacities, and ensure effective coordination between health departments and local authorities.

"Coordinated efforts between the Central Government, States/UTs, local administrations and healthcare institutions are essential to minimise disease burden and ensure timely response to emerging public health challenges."

— JP Nadda, Union Health Minister

Nadda instructed hospitals to remain fully prepared with adequate medicines, diagnostic facilities, blood components, and trained personnel. He also ordered strict adherence to standard treatment guidelines and clinical management protocols.

The Numbers Tell a Worrying Story

The scale of the challenge is evident in early data. According to the National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC), India recorded 6,927 dengue cases by the end of February 2026 — a figure that surpassed the entire January-May 2021 total of 6,837 cases within just two months. In 2025, the country reported 233,519 dengue cases, 297 deaths, and 17,930 cases of chikungunya.

As the monsoon intensifies, states are already reporting sharp spikes. Karnataka has logged 5,374 dengue cases and five deaths. Telangana reported 882 cases, while Ernakulam district in Kerala has seen 400 cases. Andhra Pradesh is dealing with concurrent dengue and malaria outbreaks, and Odisha has recorded 288 cases.

Not Just a Monsoon Disease Anymore

Health experts point to a fundamental shift in dengue epidemiology. Rising temperatures, irregular rainfall patterns, and rapid urbanisation are enabling the Aedes aegypti mosquito to survive longer and expand its geographical reach.

"Dengue is no longer restricted to the post-monsoon period. We are increasingly seeing cases outside the traditional season. The transmission window appears to be expanding," Dr Harshdeep Joshi, professor and head of Community Medicine at Maharishi Markandeshwar Medical College, told Al Jazeera.

Paediatricians in Bengaluru report that children are presenting with atypical symptoms, including upper respiratory infections and gastroenteritis, that test positive for dengue — making clinical diagnosis more challenging.

Port Surveillance and the Zika Threat

The health ministry has also directed all airports, seaports, and land ports to implement vector-borne disease surveillance and control measures. Under India's obligations as a signatory to the International Health Regulations 2005, ports are required to maintain vector-free zones.

Beyond dengue, officials are monitoring the Zika virus, which can cause birth defects when it infects pregnant women. India recorded 151 Zika cases in 2025, with Maharashtra accounting for 140 of them.

What NRIs Should Know

For diaspora members planning monsoon-season travel to India, the advisory is clear: carry insect repellent, wear protective clothing, and seek medical attention immediately for any unexplained fever. The shift toward year-round dengue transmission means the risk window has widened beyond the traditional July-November period. The government's push for digital surveillance through the Integrated Health Information Platform aims to improve real-time reporting, but public health experts warn that underreporting remains a persistent challenge.
nri_angle: NRIs travelling to India during monsoon season face an expanding dengue transmission window that now extends well beyond traditional post-monsoon months.
